catalogue.title: D2.4 Catalogue of measures for urban aquatic ecosystems rehabilitation
catalogue.authors: Dias, M., Serra, S.R.Q., Feio, M.J. (University of Coimbra)
catalogue.page_note: Page numbers are the printed document pages from the catalogue's own table of contents. In this PDF, printed page N is sheet N+2.

provenance_note: Measure names, sections and page numbers are from the catalogue. The mapping from observable problems to measures, the plain-language descriptions, the health co-benefit tags and the effort estimates are ours and are marked 'project judgement (StreamLens)'. The catalogue links rehabilitation to health in general terms at p.132 rather than measure by measure.
health_note: Co-benefit tags describe why a measure may be good for people in general terms - shade, fewer mosquito breeding sites, a place worth walking to. They are not medical claims and must never be presented as any.

measures.name: Let the bank vegetation grow back on its own
measures.plain_language: Stop mowing and clearing a strip along the bank and let whatever grows there come back by itself. The cheapest measure in the catalogue.
measures.ecosystem_benefit: Shade, bank stability, leaf litter as food, cover for animals.

source.catalogue_name: Passive riparian vegetation: allowing natural regeneration

measures.name: Replant the bank with native trees and shrubs
measures.plain_language: Plant native trees and shrubs along the bank where nothing is regenerating on its own.
measures.ecosystem_benefit: Shade that cools the water, roots that hold the bank, habitat and a corridor for wildlife.

measures.name: Keep a planted buffer strip between the town and the water
measures.plain_language: A planted strip between the built-up area and the water, even a narrow one, to filter what runs off the land.
measures.ecosystem_benefit: Filters runoff before it reaches the water; buffers the channel from what happens on the land beside it.

measures.name: Fix the sewer connections and point discharges
measures.plain_language: Find and fix misconnected or leaking pipes, and reduce discharges from the sewer network into the stream.
measures.ecosystem_benefit: Removes the pollution at source rather than treating it downstream; the first-line measure for foul water.

measures.name: Help the stream clean itself
measures.plain_language: Restore the riffles, gravels and plants that let a stream break down pollutants through its own biology.
measures.ecosystem_benefit: Higher oxygen and more biological processing of nutrients.

measures.name: Litter, plastic and oil control
measures.plain_language: Traps, screens and regular clean-ups, together with stopping litter entering from the street drains in the first place.
measures.ecosystem_benefit: Less physical harm to animals; fewer pollutants leaching into the water.

measures.name: Treat waste water with a constructed wetland
measures.plain_language: A reed bed or constructed wetland that treats waste water using plants and soil instead of a chemical plant.
measures.ecosystem_benefit: Removes nutrients and pathogens while itself being habitat.

measures.name: Floating treatment wetlands
measures.plain_language: Rafts of plants floating on the water whose roots strip out nutrients. Useful where there is no room on the bank.
measures.ecosystem_benefit: Nutrient uptake and shade in slow or standing reaches.

measures.name: Remove the barrier
measures.plain_language: Take out a weir, dam or culvert that no longer serves a purpose, so animals and sediment can move along the stream again.
measures.ecosystem_benefit: Restores movement up and down the stream for fish and invertebrates, and lets sediment through.

measures.name: Make the barrier passable
measures.plain_language: Where a barrier has to stay, add a fish pass or rock ramp so animals can still get past it.
measures.ecosystem_benefit: Partial restoration of movement where removal is not possible.

measures.name: Let the stream bend again
measures.plain_language: Give a straightened channel its bends back, so it has fast and slow stretches instead of one uniform chute.
measures.ecosystem_benefit: Varied flow and depth, which is what creates varied habitat.

measures.name: Put a natural bed back
measures.plain_language: Replace a concrete bed with gravel, stone and sediment the stream can move and sort by itself.
measures.ecosystem_benefit: Restores the spaces between stones where stream animals live.

measures.name: Build riffles
measures.plain_language: Add shallow stony stretches where water breaks over stones and picks up oxygen.
measures.ecosystem_benefit: Oxygenation and the habitat most invertebrates depend on.

measures.name: Take the hard bank facing out
measures.plain_language: Remove concrete or stone facing from the bank where it is no longer needed, and let the bank become soil and roots again.
measures.ecosystem_benefit: Reconnects the water with the bank and its wildlife.

measures.name: Reshape a steep bank to a gentle slope
measures.plain_language: Slope a steep or undercut bank back so plants can root and people can reach the water safely.
measures.ecosystem_benefit: Stable bank with a planted margin instead of a bare face.

measures.name: Live fascines (bundles of living branches)
measures.plain_language: Bundles of living willow branches laid along the bank; they root and hold the soil, replacing stone or concrete.
measures.ecosystem_benefit: Bank stability that is alive and gets stronger over time.

measures.name: Erosion control blanket
measures.plain_language: A biodegradable mat pinned over bare soil so it holds until planting takes root.
measures.ecosystem_benefit: Stops soil washing into the stream while vegetation establishes.

measures.name: Rain gardens
measures.plain_language: Planted hollows that catch road and roof runoff and let it soak away instead of rushing into the stream.
measures.ecosystem_benefit: Cuts the flashy peak after rain and filters what is in it.

measures.name: Permeable paving
measures.plain_language: Surfaces rain can soak through, instead of tarmac that sends it straight to the stream.
measures.ecosystem_benefit: Less runoff volume and less of the pollution it carries.

measures.name: Disconnect the hard surfaces from the drain
measures.plain_language: Route water from roofs and paving onto soil and planting rather than into the storm drain.
measures.ecosystem_benefit: Directly reduces the storm peak reaching the channel.

measures.name: Vegetated swales
measures.plain_language: Shallow planted channels that carry runoff slowly and clean it on the way.
measures.ecosystem_benefit: Slows and filters runoff before it reaches the stream.

measures.name: Retention ponds and floodable parks
measures.plain_language: Places designed to hold water when it rains hard - often a park that is allowed to flood.
measures.ecosystem_benefit: Storm storage, plus wetland habitat the rest of the year.

measures.name: Reconnect the floodplain
measures.plain_language: Let the stream spill onto its floodplain again instead of being held inside walls.
measures.ecosystem_benefit: Flood storage, sediment deposition and wet habitat.

measures.name: Control or remove invasive species
measures.plain_language: Remove invasive plants and replant with native species. Usually needs repeating for several years to work.
measures.ecosystem_benefit: Lets native bank vegetation and the animals that depend on it re-establish.

measures.name: Citizen science and school partnerships
measures.plain_language: Keep people watching the stream - which is what StreamLens itself is for. Sustained local attention is what keeps other measures maintained.
measures.ecosystem_benefit: Continuous monitoring and earlier detection of problems.

problems.name: Paved or hardened banks
problems.why_it_matters: A concrete or stone bank has no roots, no burrows and no plants, so the edge of the stream stops being habitat.

problems.name: Concrete or artificial bed
problems.why_it_matters: A hard flat bed has none of the gaps between stones where stream insects live, and water runs over it too fast.

problems.name: Bare or unvegetated banks
problems.why_it_matters: Without plants the water is unshaded and warmer, the bank erodes, and nothing filters what runs off the land.

problems.name: Sewage or a polluted outfall
problems.why_it_matters: Foul water strips oxygen from the stream and is the pressure most likely to matter to people living nearby.

problems.name: Barriers blocking the stream
problems.why_it_matters: A weir or culvert stops fish and invertebrates moving up and down, cutting populations off from each other.

problems.name: Litter in or beside the channel
problems.why_it_matters: Litter harms animals directly and is the strongest visible signal to residents that a stream is neglected.

problems.name: Sealed surfaces right up to the bank
problems.why_it_matters: Rain runs straight off tarmac into the stream, carrying whatever was on the surface and causing a flashy surge.

problems.name: Invasive plants on the banks
problems.why_it_matters: Species such as giant reed or knotweed crowd out native plants and leave banks bare when they die back.

problems.name: Standing or dry channel
problems.why_it_matters: Water that does not move warms up, loses oxygen and can become mosquito habitat.

problems.name: No habitat features in the water
problems.why_it_matters: A uniform channel with no stones, bars or plants supports very few species however clean the water is.
